name: 01_method_overview
prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Create a polished raster illustration for an AI research paper and conference slides, wide landscape 16:9, high resolution. Title: "Failure-Triggered World-Model Repair". Not a plain vector flowchart: sophisticated hand-rendered isometric miniature household scene, tactile matte 3D objects with delicate ink outlines, soft ambient shading, restrained academic editorial illustration. White background, generous margins, navy typography, muted blue planner, teal world model, warm coral invalid action. Precise legible short English labels only.
Composition: A clear left-to-right illustrated scientific architecture with upper direct path and lower advice detour. Left: miniature kitchen countertop with apple and a small blue embodied agent holding one tomato; adjacent context sheet labelled "Task + history + observation" and "Valid actions". Center-left blue agent labelled "Planner" proposes a small action card "Proposed action". Center a checklist labelled "Validity check" (environment-provided, BEFORE execution). Upper blue route labelled "Valid" bypasses world model and leads to right kitchen labelled "Execute". Lower coral route labelled "Invalid" leads to a teal softly rendered neural-model device labelled "Frozen world model"; two clean response cards emerge labelled "Reason" and "Suggested first step". Next a small checklist shield labelled "Validate suggestion" with tiny note "Discard invalid suggestion". Next blue planner labelled "Planner revises", arrow to the SAME right execution kitchen. Only planner connects to execution; WM does not execute. A thin bottom feedback arrow leads from execution back to the context, labelled "New observation". Use generous separation and disciplined readable arrows, no crossed arrows. Footer: "WM advises; the planner decides." Small note: "Both models frozen • No explicit rule base". In a small footnote: "'check valid actions' bypasses repair." The household vignette is illustrative, not an experimental screenshot. No results, percentages, extra charts, watermarks, fake citations or dense paragraph text. The important visual appeal is beautiful tangible scenes and expressive but professional miniature agents, balanced with scientifically exact causal routing.

name: 01_method_overview_correction
prompt: Edit this scientific illustration, preserve composition, style, all routing, characters and other text. Correct ONLY two cards: On the left clipboard, keep headers "Task + history + observation" and "Valid actions", but replace BOTH pick(tomato) and pick(apple) rows with three abstract horizontal gray lines, NO action names or check marks next to action names. On the small proposed action card between Planner and Validity check, remove tomato icon and pick(tomato) and replace with a simple document icon and text "Candidate". These abstractions must not assert any particular action is valid. Keep all other content unchanged.

name: 02_when_what_how
prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. Generate a beautiful raster research illustration, landscape 16:9, white background, high detail tactile miniature 3D scenes, soft hand-painted texture, delicate outlines, navy serif headings, blue robot planner and teal neural-model device, coral failure accents. Academic editorial illustration with generous whitespace, not generic flat vector boxes. Title "From Prediction to Repair". Three equally sized illustrated vignettes, connected by subtle left-to-right arrows. Left heading "WHEN" subtitle "When to consult?". Blue planner in miniature kitchen facing teal forecast device; elegant clock and small predicted-observation card "Nothing happens." Convey timing choices by a few clock markers. Below vignette exact two-line text "Test forecast timing" and "Limited gains in tested settings". Middle heading "WHAT" subtitle "What information helps?". Beautiful close-up of robot holding tomato and reaching toward apple on counter, a magnifying glass highlights occupied gripper; two explanatory cards "Missing precondition" and "Feasible first step". Below exact text "Probe recovery information" and "Oracle cause + first step". Right heading "HOW" subtitle "How to guide recovery?". Teal frozen model with snowflake symbol gives two cards "Reason" and "Repair" to blue planner, who chooses to place tomato down in a miniature kitchen. A small valid-action checklist upstream of model. Below exact text "Failure-triggered WM repair" and "Planner retains control". Bottom restrained statement "From forecasting consequences to supporting recovery". Small footer "Conceptual illustrations; examples are not recorded trajectories." No scores, no invented results, no claim prediction is always useless, no claim of guaranteed repair, no large decorative gradients. Keep scenes visually gorgeous but logic simple and labels large enough for slides.

name: 03_failure_loop
prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. Beautiful academic raster illustration for paper/slide, 16:9 wide landscape, pure white background, softly hand-painted matte 3D miniature kitchen scenes, blue and white robot planner, navy serif titles, teal accents and restrained coral failure arrows. Title "Why Failure Feedback Is Not Enough". Three distinct scenes arranged horizontally with a flowing coral return arrow underneath, giving an elegant readable loop. Panel 1 heading "1  Propose": a blue robot already holding ONE red tomato in its left gripper reaches unsuccessfully toward a red-and-yellow apple on a kitchen countertop with its free gripper. Small thought bubble "Take the apple". Panel 2 heading "2  Observe": SAME scene unchanged, robot STILL holding tomato and apple STILL on countertop. Large environment speech bubble "Nothing happens." Panel 3 heading "3  Repeat": same robot still holding tomato, again reaching toward apple still on countertop, puzzled expressive face, small thought bubble "Try again?". Under these panels a coral curved arrow from right back to left labelled "The missing precondition remains unresolved". Small zoomed inset in whitespace shows occupied gripper holding tomato, label "Inventory constraint". Bottom statement "Failure feedback identifies no progress, but may not explain recovery." Small footer "Illustrative example • ALFWorld text interaction visualized as a household scene". No numerical results, no successful apple pickup, no WM in this image, no invented action syntax, no dense boxes, no watermarks. Distinct visually compelling kitchen details with generous whitespace and subtle shadows; professional scientific storytelling rather than childish comic.

name: 04_repair_example
prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. Create exquisite research-paper raster illustration 16:9 landscape, white background, tactile hand-painted miniature 3D kitchen scenes, sophisticated navy serif typography, blue-and-white robot planner, teal world-model device, subtle soft shadows, same elegant editorial family as an AI planning paper. Title "From Knowing Failure to Knowing a First Step". Three illustrated panels in a clear sequence with thin arrows; broad margins. Left "Infeasible proposal": robot already holding one tomato, apple resting on countertop, robot thinks "Take the apple". Small clipboard shows "Gate: invalid proposal". No actual action is executed in this panel; the pre-execution gate detects infeasibility. Middle "World-model advice": a teal neural-model machine with small snowflake produces two beautifully typeset cards, exact text "Reason: Already holding another object." and "Repair: Put the tomato down first." Small checklist underneath reads "Check suggested step against valid actions". This advice is illustrative. Right "Planner chooses": blue robot gently puts tomato on countertop, apple remains on countertop untouched, hands now free. Small speech bubble "I will put it down first." A small lower caption "One possible revised action". Footer "Illustrative example, not a recorded trajectory. Advice does not guarantee task completion." Bottom bold takeaway "Explain the obstacle. Suggest a first step. Let the planner decide." Need pleasant realistic material detail, expressive poses, tasteful scientific storytelling. No giant abstract diagram boxes, no numeric scores, no arrows directly from world model to environment, no depiction of completed task or picking apple while holding tomato.

name: 05_interface_ablation
prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. A polished research illustration, wide 16:9, pure white background, charming but professional matte 3D editorial miniatures with softly painted textures, restrained blue/teal/navy/coral palette. Title "What Should the World Model Tell the Planner?". Two organized horizontal bands with exquisite tactile objects, readable large navy typography, lots of whitespace. TOP BAND heading "(a) Equal-information comparison". At left a stack of four beautifully illustrated papers beside a tiny kitchen vignette and tomato-holding blue robot, labelled collectively "Same inputs" with exactly four short text lines "Task + history", "Observation", "Valid actions", "Invalid proposal". This branches to two side-by-side teal miniature neural-model devices, labelled "Predict" and "Repair", connected respectively to paper response cards. Predict card exact text "Next observation" then "Nothing happens." Repair card exact text "Reason + first step" then "Already holding an object." then "Put it down first." At right a blue-and-white planner with label "Planner revises". Both response paths feed the planner. Small line under this band "Same failure gate and WM; change the requested output". BOTTOM BAND heading "(b) Component ablation". One teal WM device on left with exact label "One repair response" emits two small cards "Reason" and "Step". Then a four-way fan spreads to FOUR neat display cards laid out horizontally and clearly titled "Failure only", "Cause only", "Step only", "Cause + step". Under titles show respectively short text "Notice", "Notice + reason", "Notice + step", "Notice + both". A discreet bracket spanning ONLY the last THREE cards says "Same WM call; vary displayed fields". Failure-only is a separate control; do not place it under that bracket. Bottom small footer "Experimental design • Example messages are illustrative • No performance values shown". No charts, no invented results, no claim component arms use different WM prompts, no real screenshots, no watermarks. Convey scientific rigor with visual warmth and tangible miniature model devices, papers and robot, not a flat vector diagram.
